arrogate

AIR-uh-gayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To arrogate is to take or claim without justification.

The junior partner arrogated decisions that were never his to make.

Example

Over several quiet months, the vice president arrogated more and more of the CEO's own responsibilities.

No one gave the vice president these responsibilities -- he simply seized them for himself, which is exactly arrogate.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

hijack: To hijack is to grab control of something suddenly and by force — a plane, a meeting, a conversation — right out in the open. To arrogate is subtler: quietly claiming powers or rights you were never given, often little by little and behind a show of legitimacy. Hijacking announces itself; arrogating hides inside procedure.

commandeer: To commandeer is to take over property or resources for your own use on the spot — officials commandeer trucks in an emergency, sometimes even lawfully. To arrogate is to claim authority or rights rather than things, and never with any right to them. You commandeer a boat; you arrogate a power you mean to keep.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

relinquish: voluntarily give up control of something

Where it sits · how wrongful and sweeping the taking is — assume → arrogate → seize

assume vs. arrogate: Assuming a duty can be entirely proper and expected; arrogating it means seizing it without any right to do so.

seize vs. arrogate: Arrogate often refers to gradually claiming smaller powers or duties; to seize outright typically means taking an entire position or throne all at once.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ar-

prefix — ar-: to, toward (Latin (ad-))

root — rog

root — rog: to ask, propose (Latin (rogare))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or perform an action (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Arrogate comes from Latin ad- ('to') + rogare ('to ask, propose') + -ate -- originally 'to formally propose something for oneself,' which hardened over time into 'to simply take it.'

Use the root in a new word: interrogate

Use the root in a new word: interrogate: The same rogare root gives us interrogate (inter- 'between' + rogare, literally 'to ask between/repeatedly').

Strength Check

Word Choice

Arrogate shares its exact Latin root, rogare, with this unit's own "abrogate" -- but the two point in very different directions: arrogate means seizing power or authority for oneself, while abrogate means officially canceling an existing law or agreement.
